newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Hopes for German tax compromise grow.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Hopes for German tax compromise grow.

text.p: Hopes for a deal on Germany's planned tax reform grew on Wednesday as a representative of the opposition Social Democrats (SDP) said he could agree in principle to a significant cut in the top level of income tax.
Until now the Social Democrats have criticised such a move as a "gift to the rich" and said it would in any case be difficult to finance given the stretched state of German finances.

But earlier on Wednesday, the Cologne-based Express newspaper quoted SPD parliamentary business manager Peter Struck in an interview as saying he could accept a cut in the top tax rate from the current 53 percent to 45 percent.
In April, the party walked out of talks aimed at getting cross-party support for a new tax bill aimed at securing around 30 billion marks ($17.6 billion) of tax cuts.

Rainer Bruederle, deputy chairman of the Free Democrats (FDP), Chancellor Helmut Kohl's junior coalition partners and the most vocal supporters of tax cuts, said Struck's comments showed that the will existed among the SPD for agreement.

"It shows...that the SPD has finally moved a bit and that it must be possible within mediation talks over the summer break to come to an agreement," Bruederle said on German radio, referring to planned arbitration attempts.
Bonn wants to introduce a 39 percent top tax rate but Bruederle was earlier quoted in a newspaper as saying he would be happy with a rate of 41 percent.
The SPD controls the upper house of parliament, allowing it to resist any reform of which it does not approve.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel was reported in the mass circulation Bild newspaper to have renewed an offer to the SPD for further talks.

But, to the likely dismay of the FDP, he also reaffirmed his insistence that tax rises could not yet be ruled out because of Germany's continued problems in striving to meet single European currency deficit criteria.
"Given the financial situation, the coalition should not from the start rule out ways of covering holes in the budget," he was quoted as saying.

FDP chief Wolfgang Gerhardt, asked to comment on Bruederle's proposal as he arrived in Bonn for coalition talks later on Wednesday, said only that "it would be good if it came down as much as possible". ($ = 1.702 German Marks)
